pulls.title: logging: streamline Logger state and drop redundant methods
pulls.body:
**Problem:** The `Logger` class currently tracks enabled log messages using three separate fields:

- `m_categories` — bitmask of enabled log categories
- `m_log_level` — global log level threshold
- `m_category_log_levels` — hash map of per-category level overrides

This representation is confusing and redundant. Bitcoin Core has only ~30 log categories and 2 conditional log levels, so a mutex-protected hash map, a bitset, and a separate global level are unnecessary. The added complexity is also harmful: it makes the code harder to follow, and basic operations like setting a category's level require coordinating multiple fields and method calls.

**Solution:** This PR streamlines the `Logger` class without changing behavior, replacing the three fields with two atomics: one bitmask for each conditional log level (`Debug` and `Trace`). Each bitmask records which categories are enabled at that level.

This allows the following methods to be dropped: `EnableCategory`, `DisableCategory`, `WillLogCategory`, `LogLevel`, `SetLogLevel`, `GetCategoryMask`, `AddCategoryLogLevel`. The remaining `SetCategoryLogLevel` and `WillLogCategoryLevel` methods are now self-contained.

**Behavior note:** This is a behavior-preserving refactor with one exception: categories dynamically enabled at runtime through the `logging` RPC or the kernel `btck_logging_*` API are now always enabled at Debug level, even if `-loglevel=trace` or its kernel equivalent was set at startup. This is unlikely to matter in practice. Very little `LogTrace` logging currently exists, and both APIs are being reworked in bitcoin/bitcoin#34038 and bitcoin/bitcoin#34374. The `-loglevel` option otherwise continues to work as before when categories are not changed at runtime.

pulls.title: test: SRD tie-break test
pulls.body:
I was researching coin selection when I came across this bug, so I thought I'd fix it

Pr #33223  adjusts  weight selection to keep the lighter coin when two coins have the same value, but the test has two mistakes, as confirmed in this [comment ](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36255#discussion_r4432516127)

1. It builds `mixed_weight_pool` but passes `utxo_pool` to `TestSRDSuccess`.
2. There is nothing enforcing coin eviction because the current max weight (`4 * 3 * 67` = 804 WU) fits any two coins (544 WU)

If you reverse #33223, it still passes, which means it misses the tie-break

### The fix
The test now uses `mixed_weight_pool and adds an extra light coin so that only two light coins can fit together and evicts a coin on every tie to pass.
Lowers the max weight to 536 WU; SRD now has to evict the heavier coin on every tie to succeed

This should show failed tests with [bitcoin#33223](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/33223) reverted and pass on master.

pulls.title: wallet, rpc: Add analyzedescriptor for multisig setups
pulls.body:
Part of the multisig setup work tracked in #35645. Based on #35918 (the first 3 commits).

Before importing a multisig descriptor received from a coordinator, each participant needs to check that it is the setup they agreed on: a k-of-n where any k cosigners can spend and nothing else can, that their own key is in it, and that they all derived the same first address. Today nothing in Core reports what a descriptor commits to, so tools had to parse the descriptor string by hand, as the multisig wizard in #36325 (now closed) did.

This PR adds that check in three layers:

1. **Inspection** (commits by w0xlt, with small changes listed below): `GetKeyInfo()`, `GetKeyInventory()` and `GetPolicy()` describe a parsed descriptor's key expressions, where each key is used, and how they combine. `getdescriptorinfo` gains a `verbose` option that returns them as `keys` and `policy`.
2. **Multisig analysis, no wallet:** `AnalyzeDescriptor()` tells whether a descriptor is a recognized k-of-n setup, and if not, why. `getdescriptorinfo verbose` returns it as `analysis`, so it works even with `-disablewallet`.
3. **Wallet part:** `interfaces::Wallet::analyzeDescriptor` (for the GUI) and the `analyzedescriptor` wallet RPC add which keys the wallet holds, whether it can sign, and the first receive address. They accept any descriptor, single-sig included; `analysis.recognized` tells whether it is a safe k-of-n.

Recognized setups are `wsh(multi)`/`wsh(sortedmulti)`, and `tr(K,multi_a)`/`tr(K,sortedmulti_a)` with a single leaf, where `K` is the BIP 341 NUMS point or a `musig()` of at least k distinct cosigners. Every cosigner must be an extended key with an unhardened ranged derivation, and no two cosigners may be the same key. Anything else is still analyzed and returned, with `recognized: false` and the list of issues: the analysis warns, it never refuses a descriptor.

Example, run by one of the three cosigners:

```
$ bitcoin-cli -rpcwallet=alice analyzedescriptor "wsh(sortedmulti(2,[a1b2c3d4/48h/1h/0h/2h]tpub.../<0;1>/*,...))"
{
  "keys": [
    { "role": "ecdsa", "type": "bip32", "xpub": "tpub...", "derivation": "/0/*",
      "origin": { "master_fingerprint": "a1b2c3d4", "path": "m/48h/1h/0h/2h" }, "wallet": "mine" },
    { ..., "wallet": "not_mine" },
    { ..., "wallet": "not_mine" }
  ],
  "analysis": { "recognized": true, "shape": "wsh_multi", "sorted": true, "threshold": 2, "cosigners": [0, 1, 2], "issues": [] },
  "can_sign": true,
  "first_address": "bcrt1q..."
}
```

A **locked wallet** is not an error: a cosigner key with a hardened origin path can't be checked without the private key, so it is reported as `"unknown"`, and `can_sign` is left out unless another key is already known to be the wallet's. Everything else (`analysis`, `first_address`) is still returned, and the caller can ask the user to unlock and retry. Only the candidate private key is decrypted.

#### Commits

| | Commit | Author |
|---|---|---|
| 1‑3 | #35918 | pseudoramdom |
| 4‑7 | key/policy inspection, `getdescriptorinfo verbose` | w0xlt (see changes below) |
| 8 | `script: add AnalyzeDescriptor() for multisig setups` | co-authored with w0xlt |
| 9 | `rpc: add multisig analysis to getdescriptorinfo verbose` | |
| 10 | `wallet: add analyzeDescriptor to the wallet interface` | co-authored with w0xlt |
| 11 | `rpc: move descriptor key and analysis JSON helpers to a shared file` | move-only |
| 12 | `wallet, rpc: add analyzedescriptor` | co-authored with w0xlt |


#### Changes made to the inspection commits (4-7)

The inspection commits come from w0xlt's descriptor inspection [branch](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/compare/master...w0xlt:bitcoin:feature/descriptor-key-inspection-simplified). These changes were made on top, for w0xlt to review and agree with or not (this section will be removed once agreed):

- *script: expose key expression structure* (was "expose structured key program data")
  - Use `m_root_extkey` instead of `*GetRootExtPubKey()`.
  - The derivation test also covers `/0h/*` and `/1/*h`, checking the last-hardened and derived caches.
  - `wide += ')'` instead of `")"` in the participant test (clang-tidy `performance-prefer-single-char-overloads`).
- *script: identify descriptor key occurrences*
  - `KeyRole()` is pure virtual; descriptors without key arguments (`addr`, `raw`, `sh`, `wsh`) say so explicitly with `NONFATAL_UNREACHABLE()`.
  - Comment noting that `frame` is invalidated by the following `push_back`.
  - The walletload test mock is reduced to `return {}`.
- *script: expose descriptor policy nodes*
  - The header documents the two forms of the same construct (descriptor function vs Miniscript fragment).
  - `Assert` → `CHECK_NONFATAL`; explicit `static_cast<uint32_t>` for the threshold.
  - The fuzz target checks where each child role may appear (tap leaves only under `tr`, `script` only under `sh`/`wsh`, the Taproot internal key only on `tr`, the output key only on `rawtr`).
- *rpc: add verbose option to getdescriptorinfo*
  - The multipath note moved to the `verbose` argument help; the `policy` help explains both forms.
  - Tests for an origin without a path and for MuSig participant origins.

Open question: `script/descriptor_analysis.h` describes and gives no verdict, while `script/descriptor_analyzer.h` gives the verdict; the names are easy to mix up. Rename the first to `script/descriptor_inspection.h`?

#### Design choices

- An unrecognized descriptor claims no setup: no threshold, cosigners, sorting or key path. For example `wsh(sortedmulti(2,A,A,C))` is not a 2-of-3, since A alone can spend. Each issue lists the key IDs involved instead.
- The same xpub with different paths in two cosigner slots is a `repeated_key`, as is an xpub and its own child xpub. BIP 388 allows the same key with disjoint paths in general policies, but in a k-of-n it lets one holder fill two slots.
- A Taproot key path is either `nums` or `musig`. Any other internal key, a `musig()` of fewer than k cosigners, or one with an outsider or a repeated cosigner is `key_path_spendable`.
- For a multipath descriptor every path is analyzed and must be the same setup (`branches_differ` otherwise). `keys` and `policy` describe the first path.
- `can_sign` means the wallet holds the private key for at least one key of the descriptor, whatever its shape. Whether it is a safe k-of-n is a separate answer, `analysis.recognized`.

The functional test scenarios of #36325 were adapted here. The analysis differs from that wizard in a few places:

- `wsh(multi(...))` is recognized, with `sorted: false`: it is a valid k-of-n, and requiring `sortedmulti` was the wizard's own policy.
- A `musig()` key path of at least k distinct cosigners is recognized: those cosigners can already spend through the leaf.
- A single-path descriptor (`/0/*`) is recognized; `multipath_expansion` already shows whether it is multipath.

#### Known limits

- A cosigner key is matched against the wallet's HD keys exactly, or by deriving its origin path from the HD key with that fingerprint (normally the master key). If the wallet only holds an imported account xprv, keys below it are matched only exactly.

A release note will follow.

pulls.title: [32.x] Backports
net: defer compact filter requests that race the filter index
pulls.body:
This PR is another approach to fix a race condition bug when a yet-unconstructed compact filter is requested for an already known block.

Fixes: https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/29655, https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/27085
Related discussion: [1](https://bnoc.xyz/t/request-block-filter-peers-being-disconnected-due-to-invalid-block-requests/101/2), [2](https://github.com/lightninglabs/neutrino/issues/338)
Another approach which received NACK: https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35262

**The problem:**
Bitcoin Core receives a new block and processes it, then advertises it; however, by that moment the compact filter might not yet have been constructed. If a peer asks for a filter in that time window, Bitcoin Core simply does not respond. From the peer's perspective this is a misbehaviour (we advertised a block and don't provide filters for it), which results in disconnects or bans. While it does not critically affect core nodes, it breaks the network topology for BIP 157 clients.

More precisely, [BIP157](https://github.com/bitcoin/bips/blob/master/bip-0157.mediawiki#getcfilters) specifies that for `getcfilters` requestor:

```
StopHash MUST be known to belong to a block accepted by the receiving peer. This is the case if the peer had previously sent a headers or inv message with that block or any descendents. A node that receives getcfilters with an unknown StopHash SHOULD NOT respond.
```

Current behaviour clearly contradicts the above specification.

**Proposed solution:**

A `getcfilters`, `getcfheaders` or `getcfcheckpt` request that is racing the filter index is parked instead of being ignored:

  1. `PeerManagerImpl::ShouldDeferCFilterRequest` checks whether a request is racing the index construction: the index is synced, but has not yet caught up with the tip, and does not cover the requested stop hash yet. It never defers during IBD, where the index can lag the tip for a long time.
  2. If so, the request is stored in the peer's `m_pending_request` and we stop processing further messages from that peer. This keeps responses in order; other peers and outgoing messages are not affected.
  3. The parked request is retried whenever we process that peer's messages, at most once every 100ms (`PARKED_CF_RETRY_INTERVAL`) to avoid taking `cs_main` too often.
  4. If the request is still parked after 5s (`MAX_CF_PARK_INTERVAL`), we stop waiting and serve what we can: the peer gets the answer if the filters exist by then, otherwise the request is ignored, as it was before this PR. The peer then continues to be processed normally.


 **Tests:**

A new `cfilter_race_tests` suite (`src/test/cfilter_race_tests.cpp`) uses a `PreFilterBlocker` `CValidationInterface` registered before the filter index, so its own `BlockConnected` fires first on the scheduler thread and stalls it before the filter index gets to run `CustomAppend`. This reproduces the race window deterministically. The tests drive the real message processing path via `ConnmanTestMsg` and advance the mocked clock where time matters.

Cases covered:

  - `deferred_cfilter_response_reaches_peer` — a racing `getcfilters` is parked, not answered and not dropped, and is answered once the index catches up.
  - `deferred_cfheaders_response_reaches_peer` — the same for `getcfheaders`.
  - `pending_request_pauses_message_processing` — while a request is parked, a later `ping` from the same peer is not processed, and the responses come back in request order.
  - `parked_request_retries_are_throttled` — a parked request is not retried before the retry interval has passed, even if the filter is ready.
  - `parked_request_is_released_after_timeout` — after the park timeout the peer is no longer paused (a later `ping` is answered), and no filter is sent for a filter that does not exist.

  I've used Claude Code for this PR.

pulls.title: wallet: Allow importing of descriptors without private keys when the wallet has the private keys
pulls.body:
Currently importing a descriptor to a wallet that has private keys requires the descriptor to include the private keys. This is not ideal as it means exposing private key material. This PR makes it so that the wallet will lookup and substitute the private keys for their respective public keys in such descriptors, thus enabling importing of public descriptors into wallets with private keys.

The underlying mechanism is that the wallet retrieves all of the pubkeys from the descriptor and checks to see if any of them have private keys in any `ScriptPubKeyMan`. Additionally, if the descriptor has a xpub with key origin info, we will check if any xprvs known to the wallet have a matching fingerprint and derive to the specified xpub. If so, the origin + xpub are replaced with the single xprv with the origin derivation path prepended to the key expression's derivation path.

Possible future work is to allow the xpub substitution to work when the wallet has some child in the key origin, i.e. the wallet xprv has a key origin that is a prefix of the key origin specified for an xpub in the descriptor. Currently this kind of substitution is not being done, only root master xprvs will be substituted.

If a wallet does not have the private keys for a public descriptor, the import is still disallowed.

This PR is based on #34861 to avoid an annoying rebase.

Closes #27336

pulls.title: mining: add Block interface, fix template data race
pulls.body:
This PR catches two birds with one stone:

- fixes https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/36515
- adds a `Block` interface, which lets IPC clients fetch the block data (or its header)

This means a client can still fetch (and store) the block after `submitSolution()`, but we no longer mutate the template's `CBlock` for this.

### Block interface

`submitSolution()` no longer modifies the template. It applies the solution to a copy of the template block and returns a `Block` handle for that copy, also when the block is rejected.

`Mining::submitBlock()` and `BlockTemplate::block()` do the same. The new interface has a `data()`, `header()` and `coinbaseMerklePath()` method, so these are migrated from the `BlockTemplate` interface.

The interface can be expanded later, e.g. to tell whether the block is part of the active chain (or went stale, useful for a miner to know).

This is a breaking change for IPC clients:

- `getBlockHeader()` → `block().header()`
- `getBlock()` → `block().data()`
- `getCoinbaseMerklePath()` → `block().coinbaseMerklePath()`
- `bool submitSolution(..., reason, debug)` → `Block submitSolution(..., accepted, reason, debug)`
- `bool submitBlock(block, reason, debug)` → `Block submitBlock(block, accepted, reason, debug)`

It uses new ordinals and old methods throw.

`submitSolution()` now throws when the coinbase is null, instead of returning false.

### Performance

My agent measured how long after `submitSolution()` sv2-tp forwards the next template, with master as the baseline and an adapted sv2-tp as the client:

| Workload | Master | This PR | Paired median difference (95% CI) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Empty block | 1.32 ms | 1.40 ms | +0.05 ms [−0.11, +0.15] |
| Near-full block, 3.7 MB | 10.11 ms | 10.07 ms | −0.09 ms [−0.44, +0.28] |

The extra `block()` call costs about 0.15 ms per template for a C++ client. The alternative approach of having `submitSolution()` return the full `CBlock` added 6ms.

pulls.title: mining: use steady clock for waitNext timeout
pulls.body:
Follow up suggested in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36791#discussion_r4568050151.

`waitNext` measures its timeout and 1-second fee tick with the wall clock, while `waitTipChanged` uses the steady clock. This means a wall clock jump changes how long `waitNext` waits, and it never times out while mocktime is frozen.

Use the steady clock for the deadline and tick. `NodeClock` is kept only for the testnet 20-minute rule, which must compare node time with the tip's timestamp.

pulls.title: wallet: make descriptor SPKM mutex non-recursive
pulls.body:
Part of https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/issues/19303

This PR makes `DescriptorScriptPubKeyMan` use a non-recursive private mutex by moving locking responsibility into its public methods and using lock-held internal helpers for shared logic.

The change removes external locking of `DescriptorScriptPubKeyMan::cs_desc_man`, splits recursive internal call paths such as keypool top-up and descriptor updates, and then renames the mutex to `m_desc_mutex`.

No wallet database format, RPC behavior, keypool semantics, or external signer behavior is intended to change.

pulls.title: test: fix coinbases built on arbitrary parents
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Test helpers that attach active-tip templates to arbitrary parents retain the template's subsidy.
Existing reorg tests can pass with underpaid coinbases.
A fork crossing a halving can overpay and fail with `bad-cb-amount`.

pulls.title: refactor: extract per-message helpers from ProcessMessage (move-only)
pulls.body:
`PeerManagerImpl::ProcessMessage()` is a ~1500-line function handling every p2p message type inline, which makes it hard to navigate and review.

This PR continues splitting it into per-message helper functions, following the pattern of the recently merged fa5ab0220e02377c3c855042ecdf1f5f950d0965 (`ProcessPong()`) and fa55723b8fbd4fd056dddac5b35daf2e86021422 (`ProcessAddrs()`), as suggested by maflcko https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/34588#issuecomment-4658892004.

A preparatory commit removes the `__func__` prefix from one getheaders debug log, so moving it doesn't change the output.

Nine handlers are extracted, one move-only commit each:

  * `ProcessGetAddr()` — `getaddr`
  * `ProcessGetDataMessage()` — `getdata` (named to avoid colliding with the existing `ProcessGetData()`, which services the request queue this handler fills)
  * `ProcessGetBlocks()` — `getblocks`
  * `ProcessGetHeaders()` — `getheaders`
  * `ProcessInv()` — `inv`
  * `ProcessSendTxRcncl()` — `sendtxrcncl`
  * `ProcessTx()` — `tx`
  * `ProcessCompactBlock()` — `cmpctblock`
  * `ProcessVersion()` — `version`

Each extraction commit is a code move with indentation adjustments: the only new lines are the declaration (with thread-safety annotations), the function signature, and the one-line call site.
Each call site is `Helper(...); return;`, so `return` statements inside the moved bodies keep identical semantics. No behavior change beyond debug log output.

One final cleanup commit normalizes the remaining formatting, replaces equivalent `break` statements with `return` in `ProcessSendTxRcncl()`, and simplifies the `send_getaddr` conditional in `ProcessVersion()`.

Each extraction commit can be reviewed with the git options:
`--color-moved=dimmed-zebra --color-moved-ws=ignore-all-space`

Declarations and definitions are placed next to related existing helpers (e.g. `ProcessGetDataMessage` next to `ProcessGetData`, `ProcessGetBlocks` next to `ProcessGetBlockData`, `ProcessGetAddr` after `ProcessAddrs`).

pulls.title: mempool: remove time-based transaction expiry
pulls.body:
This is a simple mempool PR that fixes #33510.

Evicting mempool transactions by age (`-mempoolexpiry`, default two weeks) is
incentive-incompatible: it may drop transactions that could still be mined 
As discussed IRL and in #33510, this PR hence removes age-based eviction entirely.

Transactions now leave the mempool only via size limiting (`-maxmempool`),
replacement, conflicts, or inclusion in a block. The `EXPIRY` removal reason is
dropped. `-mempoolexpiry` is retained as a hidden no-op that warns when set, so
existing configurations keep starting.

Nice side effects:
- With expiry gone, the `entry_time` index has no readers. Removing it saves an
  ordered-tree node per mempool entry and drops a now unused Boost
  include.
- The `DynamicMemoryUsage()` per-entry estimate drops from three indexes to
  two, so within the same `-maxmempool` budget the mempool fits slightly more
  transactions.


I analyzed the reason=expiry evictions from a 15-node monitoring fleet (data courtesy of b10c) and checked what happened to each transaction afterwards.

Across 938,157 unique expired transactions (2024-02-16 to 2026-10-21):

- 92.0% (863,451) were later mined; only 8.0% (74,706) never confirmed.
- At least 34% (316,381) show rebroadcast evidence, and 87% of those confirmed.
- Of the ones that confirm, half are mined within about 5 days of first expiry and 90% within about 55 days.

So time-based expiry is evicting transactions that get mined anyway, usually after a rebroadcast, it costs relay bandwidth.

See thread https://bnoc.xyz/t/request-how-many-mempool-transactions-are-evicted-by-time/132

pulls.title: kernel, validation: Add btck_chainstate_manager_set_clock_time
pulls.body:
**Problem:** Kernel applications can only override the time validation uses for the whole process, with `btck_set_mock_time` (#35496). Every chainstate manager in the process sees the same time, so a time set for one test, run, or thread leaks into the others unless the application remembers to reset it.

**Solution:** Add `btck_chainstate_manager_options_set_clock_time` and `btck_chainstate_manager_set_clock_time`, which set the time for a single chainstate manager, before it is created (so it also applies to checks made while it loads the chainstate) and afterwards. Validation code gets the time from a new `ChainstateManager::Now()` method instead of calling `NodeClock::now()` directly. Details are in the commit messages.

Keeping the time in the chainstate manager instead of in a global makes kernel applications more reliable, because state from one run or thread can't affect another.

Other commits:

- The first commit fixes a rare timing race in the `chainstatemanager_ibd_exit_after_loading_blocks` test, where test code and validation code read the clock separately and assumed they got the same time.
- The last two commits switch that test and the `utxo_total_supply` fuzz target to the new per-chainman clock, as suggested in https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/35557#issuecomment-4763429282.

Two related commits that were previously part of this PR are in a follow-up branch based on it, https://github.com/ryanofsky/bitcoin/commits/pr/kclock2: a mempool refactor to represent clock times consistently, and a change that makes `NodeClock::now()` unavailable in libbitcoinkernel so kernel code can't use the system clock by accident.

pulls.title: p2p: Prefill compact blocks
pulls.body:
> ---> Review before this: #36787

This is an implementation based on 0xB10C's [proposal][proposal] and [implementation][implementation] of prefilling CMPCTBLOCK messages with what we[^1] needed during CMPCTBLOCK reconstruction in the hopes of providing everything our peers will need to reconstruct without having to ask us for transactions.

Although full support for receiving prefills is [implemented][cb-og-pr] in Bitcoin Core, the only prefills sent presently are coinbases. The goal of prefilling is to improve compact block reconstruction rates, which reduces the number of roundtrips needed to propagate blocks per-hop, which reduces the amount of time needed for blocks to propagate on the network, which mitigates selfish mining attacks by lowering the stale rate and the ratio $γ$ of honest miners a selfish miner is able to recruit in a block race.[^2] The tradeoff of prefilling is that it uses a small amount of extra bandwidth and makes propagation slightly worse when the predictions are bad.

My primary contribution is limiting the prefill based on the connection's TCP window. Exceeding the boundary of the current TCP window will result in a ~[roundtrip][roundtrip] at the network layer,[^3] and any time a roundtrip is going to be incurred anyways, it would be [better][better] to let our peer tell us exactly what they are missing in a roundtrip instead of hazarding a guess, which risks sending redundant information.[^4]

## Prefill do

In measurements I took from 2026-02-15 to 2026-03-16, a node receiving prefilled `CMPCTBLOCK`s limited to the TCP window size was able to reconstruct 89.7% of compact blocks received without a GETBLOCKTXN roundtrip, and a node receiving typical `CMPCTBLOCK`s with only coinbases prefilled was able to reconstruct 56.9% of blocks received without a GETBLOCKTXN roundtrip.[^5]

The mean prefill sent was 1,694.64 bytes and the median was 897 bytes. If all the bytes of every prefill were redundant [^6], the cost of prefilling 1,694.64 bytes would be 1.39 MiB per node in wasted bandwidth per day (counting both the sending and the receiving bandwidth for all 3 HB peers).

## Prefill why

There are changes that are likely more effective at improving propagation times than prefilling, for example:
- [Using a sketch instead of shortids][sketch-shortid] in CMPCTBLOCK messages
- Using a UDP connection with FEC as [the FIBRE project does][the-fibre-project-does]
- Sharing [block templates][block-templates]

The advantage of this approach is that it requires no protocol changes and is entirely backwards compatible with existing node software that has implemented the `CMPCTBLOCK` [protocol][protocol]. Concretely: An old version of Bitcoin Core that knows nothing about this PR can enjoy faster block reconstructions if it connects to a peer that prefills blocks. I think these benefits are worth the tradeoff of violating the layer cake and taking transport matters into our own hands.

## Prefill what

- The transactions which we were missing during reconstruction and received in a `GETBLOCKTXN->BLOCKTXN` round trip with our peer.
- The transactions which were pulled from our extrapool during reconstruction.[^7]
- Any transactions that were prefilled to us that we didn't already have in our mempool.

The reasons to like this heuristic are that it's simple, per-block rather than per-peer, makes sense on paper, and seems to be effective in practice.

## Prefill when

To avoid having to generate unique CMPCTBLOCK messages for each of our peers, which might be costly[^8], we (lazily[^9]) build and cache 2 CMPCTBLOCK messages: one prefilled and one not prefilled.

At sending time we check the available bytes in our peer's TCP window, and if the total number of TCP windows occupied by the prefilled block is equal to the total number of windows occupied by the nonprefilled block, then we send the prefilled block.

----

## TCP Windows

Discussed in greater detail [elsewhere][elsewhere], I'll try to summarize here:

In [RFC 793][rfc-793], TCP was specified with receiver advertised window sizes because receivers allocate some buffer size to a given TCP connection, and this receiver advertised window represents the most **unacknowledged** data a receiver will process before dropping bytes on the ground or something awful like that. So the sender of a message over a TCP connection will only send up to the last acknowledged byte + the receiver's advertised window size in order to avoid filling up their peer's receive buffer.

It was later discovered that TCP was susceptible to ["congestion collapse"][congestion-collapse], which can probably describe any congestion feedback loop but in TCP is where packets being dropped due to congestion results in retransmissions that cause even more congestion. TCP implementers addressed this with "congestion control" algorithms which decide on the sending side to limit the number of bytes to send dynamically, based on how frequently packets are dropped on a TCP connection. For a more concrete account of various congestion control algorithms see [RFC 5681][rfc-5681]. A user's TCP implementation (typically in their OS kernel) will compute a window size dynamically for each TCP connection usually increasing as packets sent are ACKnowledged and decreasing when packets sent are dropped.

Computed congestion control window sizes vary:
- per-connection
- over connection lifetime
- with the congestion control algorithm used by the system TCP implementation
- with user configuration of the TCP implementation.

There is not likely to be any way to guess or predict what the TCP window will be very effectively, and we must query the TCP implementation in order to learn what our connection window sizes are.

The usable window size is the smaller of the receiver advertised window and the sender computed congestion control window, but in practice the congestion control window is far smaller. In my observation node, the mean Bitcoin P2P congestion window observed was 17,360.52 bytes and the median was 14,480 bytes.

[^1]: 'We' refers to the Royal Node.
[^2]: (2013) Eyal and Sirer *Majority is not Enough* (pg. 8) https://arxiv.org/pdf/1311.0243 The claim that lowering block propagation times lowers γ probably needs serious analysis, but my hand-waving argument is that the faster public network-wide block propagation is, the more expensive any proportional propagation time advantage over the public network becomes, and γ is a function of propagation time advantage.
[^3]: A network layer roundtrip will be faster than an application layer roundtrip, although probably not by much for most connections. Since at the application layer there will be some time your message spends waiting to be processed by your peer, at least for peers that use single-threaded message processing like Bitcoin Core does presently.
[^4]: In practice exceeding the TCP window is ~not quite as bad as I've implied here and in the delving post: because the window is sliding, once the first 1.5 round-trips are completed there is a continuous stream as ACKnowledgements for the oldest segments arrive and the newest segments are fired out. The effect of this more precisely is that if a message exceeds a window boundary, the minimum travel time of the message becomes 1.5 round-trip-time (RTT) instead of 0.5 RTT and the throughput limit of the connection becomes $\text{window size} / \text{RTT}$. I am working on a more complete write-up that takes this more precise cost into consideration, but I think approximating it as a ~round trip is reasonable.
[^5]: In reality, not all of the prefill is redundant otherwise prefilling would not be very useful. In my observation node that received prefilled compact blocks, the mean redundant prefill bytes was 865.62 bytes/block. 2 HB announcements will always be redundant so: 1.17 MiB per node in wasted bandwidth per day if one CMPCTBLOCK announcement only has 865.62 redundant bytes.
[^6]: I will share a write-up describing my full experimental setup and data soon. It was mostly identical to the set up described here: https://delvingbitcoin.org/t/stats-on-compact-block-reconstructions/1052/34 I had one node running a prefilling branch, and another node set up to only receive CMPCTBLOCK messages from the prefilling node. My infrastructure as code observation set up: https://github.com/davidgumberg/prefill-research and the script I used to analyze the results: https://radicle.network/nodes/iris.radicle.network/rad:z37pH1UAxFvazXnfAMS5qbcUjQaP6/tree/leave/scripts/prefill.py
[^7]: The reason to pluck from the extrapool is because it is very likely to differ between nodes.
[^8]: But maybe there is some cost here that is worth trading off, it's not something I've explored.
[^9]: This is based on andrewtoth's #26755.

[cb-og-pr]: https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/8068

[roundtrip]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/TCP_window_scale_option#TCP_windows
[better]: https://delvingbitcoin.org/t/stats-on-compact-block-reconstructions/1052/34
[rfc-793]: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc793.html#section-2.6

pulls.title: refactor: Change some validation.cpp methods to return BlockValidationState
pulls.body:
**Summary**. Refactor validation result to be a return value instead of an output parameter in several `validation.cpp` methods.

**Motivation**. The benefits of the change are:
- Exclude the potentially inconsistent case when the bool return value and the returned `state` are inconsistent
- Exclude the ambiguity whether the passed in value of state is used or not (not obvious in chained calls)
- Remove the possibility of unintuitive interaction between subsequent calls with the same state. In case of a validation error, a failure reason is set if the state was valid, but not if it was already invalid.
- Slightly simpler: It's more evident which is the result; one less parameters.

This has grown out from #33856, mentioned in [comment here](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/33856#pullrequestreview-4276791829) and [here](https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/33856#issuecomment-4477751949).

**Details**. Many methods follow the scheme where the validation state is returned in an output parameter (`BlockValidationState& state`), and and additional `bool` return value indicating success. In success case the convention is that `state.IsValid()` and the return value are both true. After the change there is only a `BlockValidationState` return value, which is either success (`state.IsValid() == true`), or an invalid/error case.

This change is a highly localized refactor, but touching a sensitive file.

Relevant methods called by `ProcessNewBlockHeaders` and `AcceptBlock` (directly and indirectly) are touched.

Changes are separated into commits by touched methods, ordered by bottom-to-top in the call hierarchy.

pulls.title: p2p: replace full outbound peers that don't support tx relay (take 2)
pulls.body:
Picks up #28538

Outbound-full-relay slots should be used by peers that actually relay transactions, besides #28538 see #16418 and #28371 for the motivation. So try to replace peers that are not relaying txs with peers that do.

The approach differs from the original PR in a few details in response to some of the review comments there:

- A replacement is connected before the peer is evicted. The original PR disconnected a non-tx-relaying peer once all full outbound slots were filled. Reviewers preferred having a replacement available first (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/28538#issuecomment-1883481846). Now an extra outbound-full-relay connection is requested, like the extra network-specific peers, and the existing eviction of extra outbound peers prefers peers that don't relay txs.
- Peers not relaying txs don't get `m_protect`. Otherwise they could stay forever (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/28538#discussion_r1443336121), and ignoring the protection was rejected in the same thread (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/28538#discussion_r1443312604).
- An only peer on a network is not replaced. Otherwise the network-specific extra connections and this logic would keep replacing each other (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/28538#issuecomment-1883481846). This also covers the `-maxconnections=1` case (https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/28538#discussion_r1417178196).

Nothing is changed in `-blocksonly` mode or during IBD. The rename commit and the functional test are taken from the original PR with some changes to match the new behavior.

pulls.title: headersync: do parameter search at runtime
pulls.body:
This migrates the headers presync parameters (`commitment_period` and `redownload_buffer_size`) from being precomputed chainparams to being computed at runtime whenever a headers sync starts. This has as advantages:
* Less work for maintainers that need to occasionally run the current `contrib/devtools/headerssync-params.py` script.
* Less room for mistakes in that process.
* Automatically adapts based on time (as opposed to needing to predict the lifetime of the software).

To achieve this, the parameter search algorithm is implemented in C++. It is simpler, because it does not attempt to model the fact that the attacker is forced to submit their headers in batches of 2000 if they want to maintain the attack. The old Python code did that, but actually got it (slightly) wrong by missing the fact that attackers are capable of strategically deciding to stop the attack in the middle of a batch (found by darosior).

Unit tests and fuzz tests are added, and at the end the old Python code is deleted.
